content: 1. Ibrahim Khalil A, Mpunga T, Wei F, Baussano I, de Martel C, Bray F, and colleagues conducted a global analysis focusing on the age-specific burden of cervical cancer associated with HIV, with particular emphasis on sub-Saharan Africa. This study was published in the International Journal of Cancer in 2022 (Volume 150, Pages 761–772). 2. Jones J, Weiss K, and Mermin J explored the proportion of new HIV cases among men who have sex with men that can be attributed to gonorrhea and chlamydia. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2019 (Volume 46, Pages 357–363). 3. Sexton J, Garnett G, and Rottingen JA performed a meta-analysis and meta-regression to interpret variability in the impact of sexually transmitted diseases on susceptibility to HIV infection. This work appeared in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2005 (Volume 32, Pages 351–357). 4. Stelzle D, Tanaka LF, Lee KK, Khalil AI, Baussano I, Shah AS, and colleagues estimated the global burden of cervical cancer associated with HIV. Their research was published in The Lancet Global Health in 2020 (Volume 9, Pages e161–e169). 5. Wu MY, Gong HZ, Hu KR, Zheng H-Y, Wan X, and Li J conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the effect of syphilis infection on HIV acquisition. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2021 (Volume 97, Pages 525–533). 6. Arbyn M, Weiderpass E, Bruni L, de Sanjosé S, Saraiya M, Ferlay J, and colleagues provided estimates of the incidence and mortality of cervical cancer worldwide in 2018. This analysis was published in The Lancet Global Health in 2020 (Volume 8, Pages e191–e203). 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) released the second edition of its guidelines for screening and treating cervical pre-cancerous lesions to prevent cervical cancer. This document was published in Geneva in 2021 and is accessible online. 8. WHO also issued a policy brief with new recommendations on screening and treatment to prevent cervical cancer among women living with HIV. This was published in 2021 and is available online. 9. De Sanjosé S, Diaz M, Castellsagué X, Clifford G, Bruni L, Muñoz N, and colleagues conducted a meta-analysis on the worldwide prevalence and genotype distribution of cervical human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA in women with normal cytology. Their findings were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2007 (Volume 7, Pages 453–459). 10. Looker KJ, Welton NJ, Sabin KM, Dalal S, Vickerman P, Turner KM, and colleagues analyzed the global and regional contribution of herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) infection to HIV incidence. Their study was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2020 (Volume 20, Pages 240–249). 11. The WHO's 2021 Global Progress Report on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections emphasized accountability for global health sector strategies from 2016 to 2021. This report is available online. 12. WHO also outlined global health sector strategies for HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections for the period 2022–2030. These strategies are accessible online. 13. Kalichman SC, Pellowski J, and Turner C conducted a systematic review on the prevalence of sexually transmitted co-infections in people living with HIV/AIDS, highlighting implications for using HIV treatments for prevention. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2011 (Volume 87, Pages 183–190). 14. This systematic review and meta-analysis were published in JAMA Network Open in 2019 (Volume 2, Article e1917134). 15. Glynn JR, Biraro S, and Weiss HA highlighted the critical role of herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) in HIV incidence. Their study was published in AIDS in 2009 (Volume 23, Pages 1595–1598). 16. Looker KJ, Elmes JA, Gottlieb SL, Schiffer JT, Vickerman P, Turner KM, and colleagues updated a systematic review and meta-analysis on the effect of HSV-2 infection on subsequent HIV acquisition. This work appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2017 (Volume 17, Pages 1303–1316). 17. Cohen MS, Hoffman IF, Royce RA, Kazembe P, Dyer JR, Daly CC, and colleagues demonstrated a reduction in HIV-1 concentration in semen following urethritis treatment, with implications for preventing sexual transmission of HIV-1. This study was published in The Lancet in 1997 (Volume 349, Pages 1868–1873). 18. Naresh A, Beigi R, Woc-Colburn L, and Salata RA reviewed the bidirectional interactions between HIV-1 and sexually transmitted infections. Their findings were published in Infectious Diseases in Clinical Practice in 2009 (Volume 17, Pages 362–373). 19. Fan L, Yu A, Zhang D, Wang Z, and Ma P examined the consequences of HIV/syphilis co-infection on HIV viral load and immune response to antiretroviral therapy. Their study was published in Infection and Drug Resistance in 2021 (Volume 14, Pages 2851–2862). 20. WHO released recommendations for the prevention and treatment of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections among men who have sex with men and transgender individuals. This public health approach is accessible online. 21. WHO also provided guidelines for the prevention and treatment of HIV and sexually transmitted infections among sex workers in lowand middle-income countries. This document is available online. 22. WHO published a guideline on syphilis screening and treatment for pregnant women, accessible online. 23. WHO issued guidelines for managing symptomatic sexually transmitted infections, which are available online. 24. WHO consolidated HIV strategic information guidelines to enhance program monitoring and management. This document is accessible online. 25. Hutin Y, Low-Beer D, Bergeri I, Hess S, Garcia-Calleja JM, Hayashi C, and colleagues outlined key elements for HIV program managers to achieve viral hepatitis elimination by 2030. Their work was published in JMIR Public Health Surveillance in 2017 (Volume 3, Article e91). 26. Platt L, French CE, McGowan CR, Sabin K, Gower E, Trickey A, and colleagues conducted a global systematic review and meta-analysis on the prevalence and burden of hepatitis B virus (HBV) co-infection among people living with HIV. Their findings were published in Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2020 (Volume 27, Pages 294–315). 27. WHO released a global hepatitis report in 2017, which is accessible online. 28. Jin F, Dore GJ, Matthews G, Luhmann N, Macdonald V, Bajis S, and colleagues reviewed the prevalence and incidence of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in men who have sex with men. Their systematic review and meta-analysis were published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2021 (Volume 6, Pages 39–56). 29. Thomas DL, Astemborski J, Rai RM, Anania FA, Schaeffer M, Galai N, and colleagues studied the natural history of hepatitis C virus infection, considering host, viral, and environmental factors. This research was published in JAMA in 2000 (Volume 284, Pages 450–456). 30. Shepard CW, Finelli L, and Alter MJ reviewed the global epidemiology of hepatitis C virus infection. Their findings were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2005 (Volume 5, Pages 558–567). 31. Valle Tovo C, Alves de Mattos A, Ribeiro de Souza A, Ferrari de Oliveira Rigo J, Lerias de Almeida PR, Galperim B, and colleagues examined the impact of HIV infection in patients co-infected with hepatitis C virus. Their study was published in Liver International in 2007 (Volume 27, Pages 40–46). 32. Sulkowski MS reviewed viral hepatitis and HIV co-infection, with findings published in Journal of Hepatology in 2008 (Volume 48, Pages 353–367). 33. Thio CL reviewed hepatitis B and HIV co-infection, with findings published in Hepatology in 2009 (Volume 49, Pages S138–S145). 34. Easterbrook P, Sands A, and Harmanci H discussed challenges and priorities in managing HIV/HBV and HIV/HCV co-infections in resource-limited settings. Their work was published in Seminars in Liver Disease in 2012 (Volume 32, Pages 147–157). 35. Floreani A reviewed hepatitis C and pregnancy, with findings published in World Journal of Gastroenterology in 2013 (Volume 19, Pages 6714–6720). 36. Benova L, Mohamoud YA, Calvert C, and Abu-Raddad LJ conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the vertical transmission of hepatitis C virus. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2014 (Volume 59, Pages 765–773). 37. WHO provided a framework for monitoring and evaluating viral hepatitis B and C, including recommended indicators. This document is accessible online. 38. WHO issued interim guidance for country validation of viral hepatitis elimination, which is available online. 39. WHO outlined case definitions of HIV for surveillance and revised clinical staging and immunological classification of HIV-related disease in adults and children. This document is accessible online. 40. Liu G, Sharma M, Tan N, and Barnabas RV demonstrated that HIV-positive women have a higher risk of HPV infection, precancerous lesions, and cervical cancer. Their study was published in AIDS in 2018 (Volume 32, Pages 795–808). 41. Massad LS, Xie X, Burk R, Keller MJ, Minkoff H, D'Souza G, and colleagues studied the long-term cumulative detection of HPV among HIV-positive women. Their findings were published in AIDS (London, England) in 2014 (Volume 28, Page 2601). 42. Debeaudrap P, Sobngwi J, Tebeu P-M, and Clifford GM conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on residual or recurrent precancerous lesions after treatment of cervical lesions in HIV-infected women. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2019 (Volume 69, Pages 1555–1565). 43. AIDSinfo provides global data on HIV epidemiology and response, accessible online. 44. WHO released a global strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer as a public health problem, which is available online.
